newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Cater boosts Abbey offshore.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Cater boosts Abbey offshore.

text.p: British bank Abbey National on Thursday bought financial services group Cater Allen in a move that would enhance the fast development of Abbey's Treasury business by doubling offshore banking, especially with Cater's strong presence in Jersey.

The agreed deal is worth 191 million pounds ($318 million) in cash. Abbey is paying 580 pence for each ordinary Cater Allen share, a premium of 31 percent over the closing price of Cater Allen shares on June 4, the day before Cater said it was in unspecified bid talks.

"What Abbey brings to the party is its strong capital, its credit rating and a customer base that should be beneficial to Cater Allen," Abbey National chief executive Peter Birch told Reuters in an interview.
Abbey said Cater Allen would provide it with a substantial wholesale and retail deposit base together with new customers to which it could sell financial products.
"Abbey National's ambitions in these areas would be difficult to achieve organically," Birch said.
Cater said earlier on Thursday that it made pretax profits of 17.1 million pounds ($28.4 million) for the year to April 30, 1997 compared with 14.6 million pounds previously.
Cater had its origins as a discount house dealing with the Bank of England, and is still active in its traditional money market activities.
But in common with other houses, it has found it difficult to turn a profit in those markets, and has sold its futures trading operations.
Instead, it has diversified into onshore banking, where deposits are growing, and particularly offshore activity -- where it has profitable operations in Jersey and the Isle of Man.
These will fit in well with Abbey which, in addition to those two centres, also has operations in Gibraltar and Hong Kong.

Another Cater business which may have attracted Abbey is its presence in the retail share dealing market, where it owns City Deal and a few months ago added Glasgow-based stockbroker Aitken Campbell which runs its own electronic share dealing service.

Birch said many Abbey customers had shown a need for an execution only share dealing service which it will now be able to provide. The bank will also eventually pass on all its business from its registrars division to City Deal.
Abbey itself has also been busily diversifying away from its traditional savings and mortgages operations.
"Anything that continues Abbey's strategy to move away from the mortgage business is to be welcomed," said one analyst, "although this is quite a small step."

Abbey, formerly a mutual building society that floated on the stock exchange in 1989, has said it wants to reduce its dependence on the highly competitive savings and mortgage areas from which it still derives some 60 percent of earnings.
In 1996, Abbey raised its profit in treasury and offshore business by 18 percent to 256 million pounds, before integration costs, and grew assets by 14 percent to 47.8 billion.
Birch said it had added 50 staff to its Treasury operation this year and would no difficulty in absorbing Cater staff who will also see the Cater brand name maintained.
Abbey, whose shares were up 5.5p to 833.5p in a mixed banking sector, was recently linked to UK banking giant National Westminster Bank Plc.

Earlier this month, Abbey confirmed that it had been approached by NatWest, but that the talks had been terminated. Birch toiled Reuters that, contrary to press reports, he had categorically not been in favour of the NatWest approach.
($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
